items: Port exhaustion on the connecting side: ip_local_port_range is ~28k
500 conn/s × 60 s = 30k ports needed → EADDRNOTAVAIL
Memory and hash pressure, bounded by tcp_max_tw_buckets
Exceed it and the kernel logs 'TCP: time wait bucket table overflow'
Keep-alive connections and pooling — the real fix
Make the server the closer if clients exhaust ports
Widen ip_local_port_range
Add source IPs or destination ports to grow the 4-tuple space
SO_REUSEADDR on listeners is why restarts avoid 'Address already in use'
tcp_tw_reuse reuses a TIME_WAIT socket outbound when timestamps prove it safe
It does nothing for inbound connections
tcp_tw_recycle broke NAT'ed clients sharing an IP; gone since Linux 4.12
An idle connection sends nothing, so silence is unreadable
Peer quiet, peer crashed, cable pulled, NAT mapping dropped — identical
Half-open connections leak fds and memory forever
After idle, send a probe with seq one byte before SND.NXT
Deliberately old, carries no data
The peer's stack must answer with an ACK
7200 + 9×75 ≈ 2 h 11 min to notice a dead peer
Uselessly long for almost every application
Keepalive is off per socket; sysctls are only defaults
Enable with setsockopt(SO_KEEPALIVE, 1)
Override per socket: TCP_KEEPIDLE, TCP_KEEPINTVL, TCP_KEEPCNT
Always prefer per-socket over system-wide in shared environments
Behind cloud LBs or NAT: idle 60 s, interval 10 s, 3 probes
Also keeps NAT/LB idle timers (often 60-350 s) from dropping the flow
Keepalive is free and kernel-side but only proves the stack is alive
A hung app process still answers keepalives
Heartbeats prove the app lives, but cost code and bandwidth
Critical services use both
Bounds how long unacked data may stay in flight before dropping
Catches stalls keepalive never sees — keepalive only fires when idle
Classic bug: NLB/ELB silently drops the flow at its idle timeout
Both ends think it lives; the next write hangs until RTO exhaustion
TCP_NODELAY for request/response, SO_KEEPALIVE + the triplet
SO_REUSEADDR to rebind over TIME_WAIT
SO_REUSEPORT: many processes accept on one port, kernel load balances
TCP_USER_TIMEOUT and TCP_CONGESTION round it out
listen(fd, backlog) is capped by net.core.somaxconn (4096 now, long 128)
tcp_max_syn_backlog sizes the half-open queue separately
Accept-queue overflow is silent by default
Choose tcp_abort_on_overflow: 0 retries, 1 sends RST

lines: ss -tin      # cwnd, rtt, retrans, pacing rate

items: tcp_rmem / tcp_wmem are min/default/max autotuning triples
core.rmem_max / wmem_max cap explicit setsockopt values
Raise the max for high-BDP paths, keep autotuning on
Verify tcp_window_scaling, tcp_sack, tcp_timestamps are all 1
PMTU discovery needs ICMP 'fragmentation needed'
Firewalls blackholing ICMP = PMTU black hole: connects, then hangs on big packets
Mitigate with tcp_mtu_probing=1 or MSS clamping on the router
GSO/TSO/GRO/LRO show 64 KB 'segments' in tcpdump that never hit the wire
'Window Full' = sender blocked by rwnd, not by the network
Alert on TcpRetransSegs ratio, TCPTimeouts, ListenOverflows
Also TCPSynRetrans and TCPPruneCalled (receive buffer pressure)
Use nstat -az / netstat -s and Wireshark TCP Stream Graphs; tcpretrans, tcpconnlat from bcc

blocks.title: Never Tune Blind
blocks.text: One sysctl at a time, measure with the real workload, keep before/after numbers. Persist in /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf — sysctls are namespaced, so a host tweak may never reach your pods.

items: Treating one read() as one message — TCP is a byte stream, frame it
A successful write() means 'in the kernel send buffer', nothing more
Only an app-level ack proves receipt
close() flushes in the background — an RST or SO_LINGER 0 discards it silently
Setting tcp_tw_recycle=1 from a blog: breaks NAT'ed clients, gone in 4.12
Fighting TIME_WAIT instead of killing connection churn
The fix is reuse and pooling, not sysctl roulette
Keepalive at defaults: dead peers linger 2 hours
Or forgetting SO_KEEPALIVE is off entirely
Ignoring CLOSE_WAIT growth — your code, not the kernel, and it ends in EMFILE
Nagle on for a chatty protocol → 40 ms delayed-ACK stalls
Nagle off everywhere → a storm of tiny packets
Manual SO_RCVBUF/SO_SNDBUF kills autotuning and caps long-fat paths
Window Scale stripped → throughput capped at 64 KB / RTT, whatever the link
Every retransmission is not breakage — a small rate is how TCP finds bandwidth
Blaming TCP for HTTP/2 app-level head-of-line blocking; the fix is QUIC, not tuning
Testing on localhost then shipping to 150 ms RTT, 1% loss
Slow start, BDP and recovery only show teeth at real latency — emulate with tc netem

lines: tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem \
# now your LAN-perfect code shows its bugs

slides.page_title: Gotchas, and TCP vs Everything Else

items: You tolerate loss but not delay: voice, video, games
You need multicast or broadcast
You are building your own transport: QUIC, DNS, HTTP/3
QUIC rides UDP, moves reliability and CC to user space
Merges transport + TLS handshake: 1-RTT, 0-RTT on resumption
Independent streams — no cross-stream head-of-line blocking
Survives IP changes via connection IDs
QUIC costs: more CPU per byte, per-packet crypto in user space
Less mature offload support
UDP blocked or throttled on some networks
SCTP has message boundaries, multi-streaming, multi-homing
Technically superior for many uses
Middlebox support killed it outside telecom signalling and WebRTC data channels
Fresh HTTPS: 1 RTT TCP + 1 RTT TLS 1.3 (2 for TLS 1.2) + slow start ramp
Connection reuse is the single biggest performance lever

lines: 64 KB / 100 ms  = ~5 Mbps  # any link speed

items: That 5 Mbps cap is the argument for window scaling and parallel connections
Halving RTT doubles throughput
Even 0.1% loss badly hurts long paths
TCP's ordering guarantee is exactly what creates head-of-line blocking
You cannot have both without per-stream sequencing
State cost: per-connection kernel state on both ends and in middleboxes
That state is why churn is expensive and TIME_WAIT / port exhaustion are real

blocks.title: Where TCP Still Wins
blocks.text: Bulk transfer, broad middlebox compatibility, kernel offload performance, and universally available tooling.
TCP turns a lossy packet network into an ordered byte pipe: number the bytes, ack cumulatively, retransmit what's missing, and keep guessing how fast the network can go.

items: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK, 1 RTT, ISNs randomised
Options (MSS, wscale, SACK, timestamps) fixed for life at this moment
Sequence numbers count bytes; ACKs mean 'next byte expected'
SYN and FIN each consume one sequence number
rwnd protects the receiver's buffer and rides on the wire
cwnd protects the network and lives only in the sender
You send min(cwnd, rwnd)
Slow start (exponential) to ssthresh, then AIMD avoidance
Linear up, multiplicative down
CUBIC is the default; BBR models the path instead of reacting to loss
Teardown is four-way, independent per direction
First closer sits in TIME_WAIT 60 s on Linux — correct, not a leak
It protects the final ACK and kills old duplicates
Keepalive is opt-in and useless at defaults; pair it with TCP_USER_TIMEOUT
Reuse connections: kills handshake latency, TIME_WAIT, port exhaustion
TCP_NODELAY for request/response traffic
Size keepalive below your NAT and LB idle timeouts

blocks.title: The Recurring Lesson
blocks.text: Nearly every 'TCP problem' is an app not closing sockets, a middlebox stripping an option, or a timeout mismatch between layers — not the algorithms.

caption.text: Part 2 of TCP: THE FIELD HANDBOOK. Most "TCP problems" are not TCP's fault — they're an app that never called close(), a middlebox that stripped Window Scale, or a keepalive timer set above your load balancer's. This is the whole protocol on 10 pages: handshake and ISN randomisation, cumulative ACKs and SACK, RTO math, CUBIC vs BBR, the four-way close, and why TIME_WAIT is the protocol working correctly. Save it for the next incident where the graph flatlines at exactly 64 KB / RTT.
